Taking HAMLET Into Live Participatory Storytelling // enGEN3 brings audience-driven storytelling to the screen through a live generative performance of HAMLET, shaped by participants in real time. Yesterday, enGEN3 successfully tested HAMLET as a live generative performance, with participants shaping the story in real time. If you are curious about my thesis, you will like this: ”From On-Demand to Licensed Participation: The New Architecture of Entertainment.” Read here: https://lnkd.in/enxfi8Fn In “Stay,” the 1st episode of our participatory HAMLET live stream, participants entered a private moment between Hamlet and Ophelia at Elsinore. An interruption presented them with a decision. Their choices informed live prompts that influenced how the performance continued on screen. Hat tip to fal for providing access to H3 Max Director through their API, making the live generation behind this experiment possible. The audience became part of how the story unfolded. HAMLET is my near-future interpretation of Shakespeare’s Denmark. I am developing it as an authored anime series and a separate participatory co-creation live stream. They share a creative universe, while the live stream’s audience-shaped experiences remain separate from the series’ canon. That creative relationship is central to what we’re building at enGEN3 : Authored worlds that can respond. The characters, their relationships and the dramatic direction establish the creative framework. Participation opens that framework to an audience’s influence: how a character responds, what they reveal, how a decision changes the emotional direction of a scene. For creators and IP owners, the opportunity is to develop these experiences within their own worlds. A universe can support an authored series and a participatory live stream, giving audiences different ways to experience its characters and become involved in its stories. Our Turbochargers put that ambition into practice. We build an experience, invite people into it, and use what happens to inform the next stage of development. Bootstrapping kept this first episode to two minutes. We’re working toward longer episodes with more precise responses and greater scope for participation. Yesterday’s test brought that work to the screen. As we review the recordings and participant feedback, we’re taking what we learned into the next HAMLET episode, to our other IP partnerships, and the broader enGEN3 platform. Start your engine. 🏁

Really excited to kick off the first stage of our partnership between Ordinauts, By Blood + By Bone, and enGEN3 . I’ve been interested in the question of IP ownership and participation in Web3 for a long time. What happens when the people who hold a character can do more than simply hold it? What if they can develop it, create stories around it, make derivatives, and ultimately participate in the value created as a community builds around it? That’s the bigger idea we’re exploring with enGEN3. We’re starting small with Turbocharger: a 72-hour experiment where anyone can take a photo and turn themselves into an anime character in the world of By Blood + By Bone. https://lnkd.in/giC3XFUM It’s fun, but it’s also a first step toward exploring a question I think is still largely unanswered: How do we make digital ownership actually useful? Excited to see what people create. This is just the beginning.

Spent Tuesday at Pact ’s first Branded Entertainment Summit at the Royal Institution, and whilst the narrative (I hope) wasn’t new for those in the room, the detail, practical experience and mix of companies there were incredibly valuable, so thank you Aimee Shimmin and Ross Lewis 🙏 A few lines I jotted down that link to one another >> 1) film is a format and television is a behaviour > 2) TV is now just a screen, and a programme no longer needs a channel to reach its audience > 3) if you don’t understand the internet you can’t understand politics / economy / content / anything, because all of it now sits downstream from there. Gen Z & Gen Alpha have zero tolerance for being advertised or marketed to, and the only content that earns their attention is content they actively choose to watch. That means every brand (company / IP / person) now has to become a storyteller whether it planned to or not, because as one speaker summed it up, your brand is never more important than a cat video to the person scrolling. The good news...and again I hope not new news...is that we in the entertainment industry are storytellers 😎 and the commercial case for brands is already proven here in the UK, with M&S making back £5 for every £1 it spends on Cooking With The Stars on ITV. The session that set my mind racing was on agencies and production companies becoming one. For decades they sat on opposite sides of a wall, with agencies owning the brand relationship and the marketing idea while producers owned the storytelling craft, the talent and the route to broadcasters and streamers. That wall is coming down fast, with Wonderhood acquiring Elvis this summer and positioning itself as the only UK company operating as both a leading independent ad agency and premium TV producer. Surprising it’s taken this long, as the opportunity is to genuinely take the best from both sides! From production 👉 the ability to tell stories, package projects and engage commissioners, structure projects in a more commercially viable and achievable way, deliver sales and wider reach through distribution and scale production across multiple projects. From agencies 👉 the ability to strategise and build IP into campaigns, pitch directly to brands, think audience first, and build the commercial structure that makes the whole thing work on the brand’s P&L. Creators already operate like this, which was the thread running through Tuesday’s Netflix post (and thank you all for the incredible reaction to that one 🙏) and why brand budgets keep following the audience to them. A creator is their own strategist, studio, distributor and sales team, iterating in public and reading the audience in real time, and the creative companies that win over the next decade will be the ones that can do the same at scale across multiple brands, formats and markets. This is how every creative company is going to have to be structured in the future, and it’s exactly what we’re building for 👷🏗️

Jeff Canada (OpenAI) opened up his home in Japantown, San Francisco this week for our supper club. He not only opened up his home, but made us incredible bread (made with tomato sauce instead of water). We have a rule for these dinners: I either know you personally or you were nominated by somebody who will be there (and vouched to be a good hang!) I also have a little hack 🤫 I invite people I know know eachother. Kevin Liu & Pamela Morrow Parker worked together back at Twilio . And Pamela Morrow Parker and Mike Rigg have both mentored the same person. Mike Rigg and Maria Morales Doucedame are actual best friends IRL (though that was more luck than planning). Jeff Canada & Alexander DeMoulin were both speakers at RevFest and Jeff was also at Twilio post Segment acquisition. Nathan Follen interviewed Alexander DeMoulin at Fin, and they both worked with Steven Perini . Suzanna O'Donohue 's daughter works at Go Nimbly with me and Troy Conquer . These connections make it so that we all open up and feel at ease. After dessert, we hung out for over an hour catching up, talking about life, TV shows, things that we love, and, yes, the word "AI" was said. How could we not? We had Anthropic, OpenAI, and Perplexity sitting at the same table. There is nothing more magical than supper club for me. We are doing more supper clubs this year: New York and SF.
